title: Your guide to passé composé in French
summary: Learn about the passé composé in French, including when to use it, how it’s conjugated, and examples using common regular and irregular verbs.
body_markdown:
The *passé composé* is one of the most important verb tenses in French, but it can be confusing for learners! In this guide, we’ll tell you all about passé composé conjugation, as well as when to use it, and important exceptions.


### In this post:


- What is the passé composé?
- How do you conjugate passé composé?


- Forming the past participle


- Passé composé with avoir
- Passé composé with être


- Agreement with the past participle


- Verbs that can take avoir or être
- Negation of passé composé
- Examples of regular past participles
- Examples of irregular past participles


## What is the passé composé?


The *passé composé* is one way to talk about things in the past in French, and it’s an important one to know! For example, the phrase J’ai mangé


, from manger


(to eat) can be used as the equivalent of any of these three English phrases:


- I ate
- I did eat
- I have eaten


## How do you conjugate passé composé?


The passé composé requires two parts: an **auxiliary verb** , and the **past participle** of the verb you want to use. For example, the past participle of *eat* is *eaten* .


The auxiliary verb, or “helping verb,” is always either avoir


(to have) or être


(to be). Most verbs takeavoir , whileêtre is limited to certain verbs and certain verb forms.


### Forming the past participle


French verbs are divided into three categories, depending on the last two letters of their infinitive form: *-er* verbs, *-ir* verbs, and *-re* verbs. **Regular** past participles of each of these verb categories are formed as follows:


*-er* verbs *-ir* verbs *-re* verbs


Infinitive manger


to eat finir


to finish attendre


to wait (for)


Past participle mangé


fini


attendu


Example sentence J’ai mangé des pâtes.


I ate pasta. J’ai fini mes devoirs.


I finished my homework. J’ai attendu le bus.


I waited for the bus.


There are also many important irregular past participles to learn. Check out our table ofcommon irregular past participles at the end of this post!


## Passé composé with *avoir*


Most verbs use the auxiliary verb *avoir* in passé composé. Here’s how it looks with the verb fermer


(to close):

Elles ont fermé la fenêtre.

## Passé composé with *être*


A small number of verbs use *être* instead of *avoir* as an auxiliary verb, and you can remember them using the DR. & MRS. VANDERTRAMPP acronym:


Here are the past participles for all of the “Dr. & Mrs. Vandertrampp” verbs that take *être* in the passé composé:

Je suis venu parce que je voulais te voir.

I fell, but I’m not injured.

I left the park around ten o’clock.


passer

Je suis passé par ton bureau ce matin.


I passed by your office this morning.


### Agreement with the past participle


There’s one more important thing to know about the past participles above that go with *être* in the passé composé: If the subject is[feminine](https://blog.duolingo.com/learning-grammatical-gender-rules/#tips-for-grammatical-gender-in-french) or plural, their endings change to reflect this!


Original sentence Subject New sentence Subject


Je suis devenu comptable.


I became an accountant.


masculine, singular Je suis devenue comptable.


I became an accountant.


feminine, singular


Je suis sorti me balader.


I went out to go for a walk.


masculine, singular Nous sommes sortis nous balader.


We went out to go for a walk.


masculine, plural


Je suis né à Paris.


I was born in Paris.


masculine, singular Nous sommes nées à Paris.


We were born in Paris.


feminine, plural

## Verbs that can take *avoir* or *être*


### Transitive vs. intransitive verbs


Even though the “Dr. & Mrs. Vandertrampp” verbs generally take *être* , there **is** one context where they take *avoir* instead: If they have a **direct object** (in other words, if they’re **transitive** ), they’ll go with *avoir* !


Here are some examples:


Intransitive verb with *être* Transitive verb with *avoir*


Je suis monté au quatrième étage.


I went up to the fourth floor. J’ai monté l’escalier jusqu’au quatrième étage.


I went up the stairs to the fourth floor.


**Direct object:** *l’escalier* (the stairs)


Je suis sorti me balader.


I went out to go for a walk. J’ai sorti la voiture du garage.


I took the car out of the garage.


**Direct object:** *la voiture* (the car)


Je suis passé par ton bureau ce matin.


I passed by your office this morning. J’ai passé du temps avec mon frère.


I spent time with my brother.


**Direct object:** *du temps* (time)


### Pronominal verbs


There is also one context in which verbs that typically take *avoir* in the passé composé take *être* instead: when they become **reflexive** or **reciprocal** (together, these are called **pronominal verbs** )—in other words, when the subject and the direct object are the **same person or thing** .


For example, Je lave la vaisselle


(I wash the dishes) **isn’t** reflexive—the subject is *je* (I) and the direct object is *la vaisselle* (the dishes), but Je me lave les cheveux


(I wash my hair) **is** reflexive in French, because the subject is *je* (I), and the object— *mes cheveux* (my hair)—is something that inextricably belongs to you.


Reciprocal verbs work similarly: J’aime mon chien


(I love my dog) **isn’t** reciprocal, because the subject is *je* (I) and the direct object is *mon chien* (my dog), but Mon chat et mon chien s’aiment


(My cat and my dog love each other) **is** reciprocal, because *mon chat* (my cat) and *mon chien* (my dog) represent both the subjects and the direct objects of the sentence.


**Note:** When a pronominal verb is in the passé composé, the past participle has to agree with the subject, just likeany other verb that uses être in the passé composé!


Here are some examples of how this works in the passé composé:


Non-pronominal verbs with *avoir* Pronominal verbs with *être*


J’ai regardé les photos.


I looked at the photos. Je me suis regardée dans le miroir.


I looked at myself in the mirror.


Tu as cassé la fenêtre.


You broke the window. Tu t’es cassé le bras.


You broke your \[own\] arm.


Elle a réveillé sa colocataire.


She woke up her roommate. Elle s’est réveillée à huit heures.


She woke \[herself\] up at eight o’clock.


Nous avons compris la leçon.


We understood the lesson. Nous nous sommes compris immédiatement.


We immediately understood each other.


Vous avez rencontré ma tante.


You (all) met my aunt. Vous vous êtes rencontrés en 2007.


You (all) met each other in 2007.


Elles ont téléphoné au maire.


They called the mayor. Elles se sont téléphonées tous les jours.


They called each other every day.


## Negation of passé composé


Now we know how to talk about what *did* happen in the past, but what about what *didn’t* happen? Since the passé composé requires two different parts (a form of *avoir* or *être* , plus a past participle), **negation** in the passé composé works a little bit differently than in many other tenses!


💡


The general rule for negation in the passé composé is to put **ne** and **pas** on either side of the auxiliary verb ( **avoir** or **être** ).


If there’s an object pronoun in the sentence, like me


( *me* or *to me* ), te


( *you* or *to you* ), etc., those go after the *ne* as well!


Here are some examples:


Affirmative passé composé Negated passé composé


Alice a écrit un livre.


Alice wrote a book. Alice n’a pas écrit un livre.


Alice didn’t write a book.


Paolo est parti tôt.


Paolo left early. Paolo n’est pas parti tôt.


Paolo didn’t leave early.


Hélène m’a parlé.


Hélène talked to me. Hélène ne m’a pas parlé.


Hélène didn’t talk to me.


Laurent s’est brossé les dents.


Laurent brushed his teeth. Laurent ne s’est pas brossé les dents.


Laurent didn’t brush his teeth.


But there are other important negation phrases besides *ne… pas* ! There’s ne… jamais


(never), ne… plus


(not anymore), ne… rien


(nothing), ne… que


(only, no more than), and ne… personne


(nobody). Of these, *ne… jamais* , *ne… plus* , and *ne… rien* go around the auxiliary verb **only** , while *ne… que* and *ne… personne* go around the auxiliary verb **and** the past participle. Here are some examples:


Affirmative passé composé Negated passé composé Position of negation


Marie est allée en Italie.


Marie went to Italy. Marie n’est jamais allée en Italie.


Marie never went to Italy. Around *être* or *avoir* **only**


Karim est retourné au Canada.


Karim went back to Canada. Karim n’est plus retourné au Canada.


Karim didn’t go back to Canada anymore.


Sandrine a cuisiné ce plat.


Sandrine cooked this dish. Sandrine n’a rien cuisiné.


Sandrine didn’t cook anything.


Antoine a lu trois livres.


Antoine read three books. Antoine n’a lu que trois livres.


Antoine only read three books. Around *être* or *avoir* **and** the past participle


Céline a vu sa famille.


Céline saw her family. Céline n’a vu personne.


Céline didn’t see anybody.


**Note:** Remember that you’re most likely to see *ne* in written or formal French.[It’s often dropped](https://blog.duolingo.com/french-language-predictions/#%F0%9F%94%AE-prediction-1-you-are-pas-going-to-believe-this) in everyday, casual, or spoken French!


## Leave your doubts in the *passé* !


The passé composé might seem like a lot of rules, but the more you practice, the easier it gets! And you can refer to this post or any of our other tips for learning French whenever you need a refresher 😉
